Ordering all the new stock from a different supplier each month

options: Wear gloves, keep it apart, and clean up as the SDS says

essays.stem: Describe the steps to receive a mixed delivery of food and cleaning supplies at a villa.
essays.modelAnswer: Before the delivery comes, I make space in the stores, have the purchase order ready, and get a trolley, a clean probe thermometer and a pen. I wash my hands. When the driver arrives, I check the delivery is for our villa. I check the chilled and frozen food first, so it is not left out: I check the temperature with the probe thermometer and look for signs of thawing. Then I check every item against the purchase order and the delivery note: the right item, the right quantity, the right size and the price if shown. I check the quality and condition, looking for damaged boxes, dented or blown cans, leaking chemicals and torn packets, and I check the use-by and best-before dates. I record any shortages, damage or rejected items on the delivery note, and the driver and I both sign it. Then I put away chilled and frozen food straight away, then dry goods, then chemicals in their own locked store. Last, I record the stock and pass the paperwork on.
markingPoints: Prepares space, paperwork, thermometer and trolley; washes hands
Checks chilled and frozen items first, with a thermometer
Checks items, quantities and prices against the purchase order and delivery note
Checks condition and dates, records problems and signs with the driver
Puts away chilled and frozen first, chemicals separately, then records the stock

essays.stem: Explain how to check chilled and frozen food on delivery, and what to do if it fails the check.
essays.modelAnswer: Chilled and frozen food can grow harmful bacteria if it gets warm, so it is checked first and quickly. I use a clean probe thermometer that has been checked, and I wipe it with a probe wipe before and after use. For packed food I can put the probe between two packs so I do not open them. Chilled food should be at 5 °C or below, or as the property's food safety plan says. Frozen food should be frozen hard, with no soft patches, water or ice crystals in the box, which show it has thawed and may have been refrozen. I look at the van too: it should be clean and cold. I also check packaging is clean and not torn, and that the dates are good. If the food is too warm, thawing, damaged or out of date, I reject it. I write the reason and the temperature on the delivery note, and the driver signs it. I tell my supervisor, so the item can be reordered and a credit note asked for. Accepted food goes straight into the fridge or freezer.
markingPoints: Explains why: bacteria grow when food warms
Uses a clean, checked probe thermometer, between packs where possible
Chilled at 5 °C or below; frozen hard with no signs of thawing
Checks the van, packaging and dates
Rejects failed items, records the reason and temperature, has the driver sign, tells the supervisor

essays.stem: Explain what you would do when a delivery is short, has the wrong items, has damaged goods or has goods out of date.
essays.modelAnswer: I always check before I sign, because my signature says the goods arrived as listed. If the delivery is short, for example 8 cases of water instead of 10, I write the number actually received on the delivery note and ask the driver to sign beside it. If wrong items have come, such as the wrong size of rubbish bags or a different product from the one ordered, I do not accept them unless my supervisor agrees, and I send them back with the driver, noting it on the delivery note. Damaged goods, such as crushed boxes, broken bottles, leaking chemicals, or dented, rusty or blown cans, are rejected and recorded. Goods that are out of date, or too close to their date for us to use in time, are rejected too. In every case I keep a copy of the signed note, tell my supervisor at once, and make sure the supplier is asked for a credit note or a new delivery, so the villa does not pay for goods it did not get.
markingPoints: Checks before signing and explains why
Short delivery: records the actual quantity, driver signs
Wrong items returned unless the supervisor agrees
Damaged or out-of-date goods rejected and recorded
Keeps a copy, tells the supervisor and gets a credit note or replacement

essays.stem: Explain what stock rotation is, and how you would rotate stock when putting away a delivery.
essays.modelAnswer: Stock rotation means using older stock before newer stock, so nothing goes out of date and is wasted. The usual method is FIFO, first in, first out: the stock that came in first is used first. For food and other dated items, FEFO, first expired, first out, is also used: the item with the nearest date is used first, even if it came in later. When I put away a delivery, I first check the dates on the new stock and on the stock already on the shelf. I bring the older stock forward to the front of the shelf, and I put the new stock behind it. If the new stock has an earlier date, I put it in front instead. I make sure each item is labelled, and that food moved into store containers is labelled with its name and the date. I do not mix old and new loose food in one container. I check dates regularly and report anything near its date, so it can be used first.
markingPoints: Explains stock rotation and why it matters
Explains FIFO
Explains FEFO for dated items
New stock goes behind older stock after checking dates
Labels and dates containers, does not mix old and new, checks dates regularly

essays.stem: Describe how to store each of these in a hotel: dry food, chilled food, frozen food, cleaning chemicals, linen and guest amenities, and liquor.
essays.modelAnswer: Dry food, such as rice, flour, canned ackee and sugar, goes in a cool, dry, clean dry store, on shelves off the floor, in closed containers that are labelled and dated, and away from strong smells. Chilled food goes in the fridge or cool room at 5 °C or below, or as the food safety plan says, covered and labelled, with raw meat and fish on the bottom shelves below ready-to-eat food. Frozen food goes in the freezer at about -18 °C or colder, wrapped and dated, and is not refrozen once thawed. Cleaning chemicals go in their own locked store, away from food and linen, in their original labelled containers, with lids closed and the heaviest and most dangerous on low shelves. Clean linen and guest amenities go in a clean, dry, aired store on shelves, folded and stacked by type, away from damp and pests. Liquor and other valuable stock go in a locked store with limited key holders, and they are issued only against a signed requisition.
markingPoints: Dry food: cool, dry, off the floor, labelled and dated
Chilled: 5 °C or below, covered, raw food below ready-to-eat
Frozen: about -18 °C or colder, wrapped and dated, not refrozen
Chemicals: separate locked store, original containers, low shelves
Linen and amenities clean and dry; liquor locked and issued by requisition

essays.stem: Explain how stock records are kept in a villa or hotel store.
essays.modelAnswer: Every item in the store has a record, either a stock card (bin card) on the shelf or an entry in a computer stock system. When a delivery is accepted, the amount received is added, with the date and the delivery note number. When stock is issued, it is only given out against a signed requisition from the department, and the amount is taken off the record, with the date and who it went to. The record then shows the balance left. For example, if the card shows 24 bottles of shampoo, 36 are received and 12 are issued, the balance is 48. At set times, such as the end of each month, a stocktake is done: all the stock is counted and the count is compared with the records. Any difference is recounted and reported to the supervisor, who looks into it. Records must be written clearly and on time, because they show what the villa has, help stop theft and waste, and show when to reorder.
markingPoints: A stock card or system record for each item
Receipts added with date and delivery note number
Issues only against a signed requisition, then deducted
Balance worked out correctly
Regular stocktake, differences recounted and reported; explains why records matter

essays.stem: Explain how to keep a hotel store room secure.
essays.modelAnswer: Stores hold valuable stock such as liquor, food, linen, amenities and chemicals, so they must be kept secure. The store is kept locked when no one is working in it, even for a short time. Only named staff hold keys, and keys are signed in and out in the key log and never lent or left in the door. Stock is only issued against a signed requisition, and the amount is recorded. No one helps themselves, even a co-worker or a friend. Deliveries are checked and put away straight away, not left in a corridor or at the gate. Delivery drivers and visitors are not left alone in the store. Liquor and high-value items may be kept in an extra locked cage or cupboard, with tighter records. Regular stocktakes help to show if anything is missing. Any broken lock, missing key, open door or difference in stock is reported to the supervisor or security at once.
markingPoints: Store locked when unattended
Key control: named holders, key log, never lent
Issues only by signed requisition and recorded
Deliveries put away promptly; drivers and visitors not left alone; extra security for high-value stock
Stocktakes and reporting of broken locks, lost keys or differences

essays.stem: Explain the main safety points when receiving and storing stock.
essays.modelAnswer: Manual handling is the biggest risk. Before lifting, I check the weight and get help or use a sack truck or trolley for heavy items such as 20 kg bags of rice or cases of drinks. I bend my knees, keep my back straight, hold the load close and do not twist. I store heavy items on low shelves. I wear safety shoes in case something drops on my feet. When opening boxes with a box cutter, I cut away from my body with a shallow cut and close the blade after use. To reach high shelves I use a checked step stool or stepladder, never the shelves themselves or a box. Chemicals must be handled as the label and SDS say: I wear gloves, keep leaking containers apart, clean spills as the SDS says, and never mix products such as bleach and ammonia. I keep walkways and fire exits clear of boxes and flatten empty cartons. Cold rooms must have a door that opens from the inside, and I wear warm clothing if I work in them for long.
markingPoints: Safe lifting, with help or a sack truck or trolley; heavy items low
Safety shoes and safe use of box cutters
Uses a checked step stool or stepladder for high shelves
Handles chemicals and spills as the label and SDS say, never mixing
Keeps walkways and exits clear; cold room safety

essays.stem: Explain how to keep a dry store clean and free from pests.
essays.modelAnswer: A dry store must be clean, cool, dry and well aired. I sweep and mop the floor often, and I clean the shelves on a schedule, moving stock out to do it. I wipe up spills, such as flour, sugar or rice, at once, because they draw ants, cockroaches and rats. All stock is kept on shelves off the floor and away from the walls, so I can clean under and behind it and see any signs of pests. Opened packets are put into clean containers with tight lids, labelled and dated. I check deliveries for pests before they go into the store, and I do not keep cardboard boxes longer than needed, because cockroaches hide in them. Doors are kept shut, and screens, door seals and gaps are checked. I look for signs of pests, such as droppings, gnawed packets, holes, webs, dead insects or a smell. If I see any, I remove the damaged stock, keep a record, and report it at once so pest control can deal with it. I never put poison near food myself.
markingPoints: Regular cleaning of floors and shelves; spills cleaned at once
Stock off the floor and away from walls
Opened food in labelled, lidded containers; cardboard removed
Doors, screens and gaps kept closed; deliveries checked
Knows the signs of pests, removes damaged stock and reports to pest control, no poison by staff

essays.stem: Explain how a villa decides when and how much stock to reorder, including during the busy tourist season.
essays.modelAnswer: Each item has a reorder level, the lowest amount it can fall to before new stock must be ordered. This allows for the lead time, which is how long the supplier takes to deliver. Each item may also have a maximum level, so the store does not order more than it has space for or can use before the date. When the stock card or system shows an item has reached its reorder level, the store person tells the supervisor or raises an order, as the property's rules say. The amount to order is enough to bring stock back up to the maximum. Usage is checked from the stock records. In Jamaica, the winter tourist season, roughly from December to April, and holidays such as Christmas and Easter bring more guests, so more food, drinks, linen and amenities are used, and suppliers may be slower. The villa raises its levels and orders earlier before these busy times, and lowers them again in quieter months, so it does not run out or waste stock.
markingPoints: Explains the reorder level
Allows for the supplier's lead time
Uses a maximum level and stock records to decide how much
Follows the property's rules for raising an order
Plans for busy seasons and holidays, and lowers levels in quiet months

practical1.title: Receive a mixed delivery and check it against the paperwork
practical1.brief: As a group, receive a mixed delivery for the Centre's mock villa. The assessor sets up the delivery and acts as the driver. It includes boxes of dry food, a cool box of chilled items with a stated or measured temperature (real items from the Centre's kitchen, or mock items), some cleaning chemicals and a pack of towels, with a purchase order and a delivery note. Some problems are hidden in it, for example a short count, a dented or blown can, an item past its date, a wrong item, a leaking bottle and a chilled item that is too warm. Work in these stages: (1) prepare the space, paperwork, trolley and a clean probe thermometer, and wash your hands; (2) check the chilled items first and record their temperatures; (3) check every item against the purchase order and the delivery note; (4) check condition and dates; (5) write every problem on the delivery note and agree it with the driver, then sign; (6) put the accepted goods away in the right places, chilled first; (7) fill in a short delivery report for the supervisor. Every member checks at least one part of the delivery and puts at least one item away while the assessor watches. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group.
materials: A mock delivery with hidden problems, set up by the assessor
A purchase order and a delivery note
A clean probe thermometer and probe wipes
Gloves and a spill kit or cloths for the leaking bottle
A phone or camera for the photos
photos: The prepared receiving area, paperwork and thermometer
The temperature check on the chilled items
The goods laid out and checked against the paperwork
Each problem found, such as the short count, damaged can and out-of-date item
The delivery note with the problems written on and signed
The chilled items in the fridge and the dry goods and chemicals in their stores
checklist: Prepared the area, paperwork and equipment before the delivery
Checked the chilled items first with a clean probe thermometer and recorded the temperatures
Checked items and quantities against the purchase order and delivery note
Found damaged, wrong and out-of-date items and the leaking bottle
Recorded every problem correctly and signed only after checking
Put away chilled items first, then dry goods, with chemicals in their own store
Lifted and moved goods safely, using the trolley
Took a full part in the group and spoke politely to the driver
safety: Lift with bent knees, keep loads close, and use a trolley or sack truck for heavy items
Wear gloves to handle the leaking bottle; keep it apart and clean up as the SDS says
Wash hands before handling food; wipe the probe before and after each use
Keep chemicals away from food at all times; follow the maker's instructions and the Centre's rules
Cut boxes open away from your body, and close the blade after use

practical2.title: Organise a store room and carry out a stocktake
practical2.brief: As a group, organise the Centre's store room or the mock villa's store, and carry out a stocktake. The assessor sets up the store with mixed stock (dry food, cleaning chemicals, linen and guest amenities) placed badly, with some items out of date order, stock cards for each item, and a set of signed requisitions and delivery notes for the week. Work in these stages: (1) draw a plan of the store showing where each kind of stock should go (food, chemicals, linen and amenities, heavy items low); (2) clear and clean one bay of shelves at a time; (3) put the stock back to your plan, rotating it so the oldest or nearest date is at the front, and label and date containers; (4) set aside any damaged or out-of-date items and record them; (5) update the stock cards from the requisitions and delivery notes; (6) count all the stock and compare the count with the cards; (7) recount any differences and write a stocktake report, listing differences and items at or below their reorder level. Every member organises at least one bay and counts at least one group of items while the assessor watches. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical. Hand in once for the whole group.
materials: A store room with mixed stock, set up by the assessor
Stock cards, requisitions and delivery notes
Labels, a marker, chart paper and a clipboard
Cleaning cloths, a neutral cleaner, a broom and a mop
A phone or camera for the photos
photos: The group's store plan on chart paper
Stock back on the shelves, rotated, with labels facing out
Chemicals stored apart and low, away from food and linen
The updated stock cards and the count sheet
The finished store and the stocktake report
checklist: Drew a sensible plan that keeps food, chemicals and linen apart, with heavy items low
Cleaned shelves before putting stock back
Rotated stock correctly (first in, first out, or first expired, first out)
Found and recorded damaged and out-of-date items
Updated the stock cards correctly from the paperwork
Wrote a clear stocktake report, including items to reorder
Worked safely, used the step stool correctly and took a full part in the group
safety: Use the checked step stool for high shelves; never climb the shelving
Lift with bent knees and get help with heavy cases
Wear gloves to move chemicals, and never store them above food or linen
Keep walkways and the store door clear while you work
Report signs of pests; do not put down poison
